title: Fui, fiz, tive — the rebellious past tense
goal: Round off the past tense with the most common irregular verbs — including one big surprise: *ser* and *ir* share **exactly the same** past forms.
bekal: giving the past forms of *ser/ir*, *estar*, *ter*, *fazer*, *ver* and *vir*
recognizing the large group patterned on *-ive* and *-isse*

notes: **Fui means both "I went" and "I was".** *Ser* and *ir* use exactly the same set of past forms: *fui, foste, foi, fomos, foram*. It's a historical accident, and it's almost never confusing — because *ir* is nearly always followed by a preposition of place. *Fui ao Porto* = I went. *Foi ótimo* = it was great.

**Foi ótimo, foi barata** — *foi* is also used without a clear subject, to judge something that's over: "it was great", "it was cheap". If the thing being judged is feminine, the adjective follows: *foi barata* (the guesthouse), *foi caro* (the trip).
**Tive de dormir** — *ter de* in the past means "had to": *tive de sair cedo* = I had to leave early.
**A seguir** means "afterwards" or "next", and is used constantly in Portugal: *a seguir ao almoço* (after lunch), *o que vem a seguir?* (what comes next?).
**Trouxe is pronounced TROH-suh**, with the *x* sounding like *s*. This is the only group of words where *x* sounds like that, and they all come from *trazer*: *trouxe*, *trouxeste*, *trouxeram*.
**A francesinha is a Porto sandwich** stuffed with meat, covered in melted cheese and drenched in a spicy beer sauce. Its name means "little French girl". It really is as heavy as Budi says.

grammars.title: Ser and ir — one past tense for two verbs
body: Learn it once, get two. It's one of the biggest savings in all of Portuguese.
after: The only thing that tells them apart is what comes next. If there's a preposition of place (*a*, *ao*, *para*), it's *ir*. If there's an adjective or a noun, it's *ser*.
Note that *foi* also appears in some very common questions: *Como foi?* ("how did it go?") and *Quando foi?* ("when was that?").

grammars.title: The big group: estar, ter, fazer, poder, saber, querer
body: These six verbs share one pattern: the *eu* form ends in an unstressed **-e**, and so does the *ele* form. Once you spot the pattern, all six fall into place together.
after: **Notice that the stress shifts forward.** *Estive* is pronounced ish-TEEV, *tive* is TEEV, *fiz* is fish. The *eu* and *ele* forms of *saber* and *querer* are **exactly the same** — *soube*, *quis* — so context tells them apart.
**Saber in the past means "found out", not "knew".** *Soube ontem* = "I only found out yesterday". Likewise *quis* means "wanted to and did", and *não quis* means "refused".
*Dizer* and *trazer* follow a similar pattern: *disse, disseste, disse, dissemos, disseram*; *trouxe, trouxeste, trouxe, trouxemos, trouxeram*.

grammars.title: Ver, vir, dar
body: Three short verbs whose past forms must be learned separately — and which turn up in almost every story.
after: **Vimos means two things:** "we saw" (past of *ver*) and "we come" (present of *vir*). Once again, context saves the day.

*Dar* appears in many fixed expressions: *dar um passeio* (to go for a walk), *dar uma volta* (to take a stroll), *dá para...?* ("is it possible to...?"). The last one is very typical of everyday speech: *Dá para ajudar?*

sections.title: Quick summary: all the irregular past forms

blocks.text: Thirteen verbs, and that's the **entire** list you really need to memorize at A1. Every other verb — hundreds of them — follows the regular patterns from unit 14. Compare English, with well over a hundred irregular verbs; Portuguese gets off lightly here.

blocks.title: How to practice without memorizing tables
items: Tell the story of your day out loud, every evening, for one week. Five sentences are enough: *Ontem acordei..., fui..., comi..., vi..., deitei-me...*
Notice that you'll need just two forms from the table above most of the time: *eu* and *ele/ela*. Master those two columns first, and the rest will follow.
If you forget a form mid-story, don't stop — use a different, regular verb. *Não pude ir* can become *não consegui ir*, and nobody will think it's wrong.
